power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = "p<0.01", Text = "Pairwise comparisons using DeLong's test confirmed the superiority of serum BD-tau over each comparator biomarker (all p<0.01)."), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::

text.text: In a multi-cohort assessment of 342 patients admitted to the neuro-intensive care unit (285 with TBI, 57 with SCI), and 22 controls, baseline serum BD-tau concentrations were markedly elevated in TBI compared with SCI, discriminating between the two populations with high accuracy (area under the curve [AUC]=0.91, 95%CI 0.87-0.96).
In paired serum-cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) samples, serum BD-tau significantly outperformed CSF BD-tau for injury-type discrimination (AUC=0.95, 95%CI 0.89-0.99 vs.

Baseline serum BD-tau also showed superior discrimination of TBI from SCI compared with established blood biomarkers of neurotrauma, including neurofilament light chain, glial fibrillary acidic protein, and ubiquitin C-terminal hydrolase L1 (AUC=0.82, 95%CI 0.76-0.88; vs.
Longitudinally, serum BD-tau remained persistently elevated in TBI, but not SCI, for up to 144 hours post-injury, with distinct temporal trajectories between injury types.

Together, these findings indicate that serum BD-tau enables rapid and minimally invasive differentiation of TBI from SCI and may support early clinical decision-making, triage, and enrollment into injury-specific therapeutic trials, highlighting the potential of circulating biomarkers to improve precision diagnostics in acute neurotrauma care.

Traumatic brain injury (TBI) and spinal cord injury (SCI) are the first and second leading causes of disability and morbidity in the United States. [5] [6] [7] The gold standard methods to assess injury severity and classification are the Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score and Computed Tomography (CT) neuroimaging for TBI and the American Spinal Injury Association (ASIA) Impairment scale for SCI [8] [9] [10] .

text.text: Blood-based biomarkers show promise for improving diagnosis, longitudinal monitoring and prognosis of patients with TBI and SCI. 17, 18 Several blood biomarkers that reflect the complex and dynamic acute pathophysiology and temporal trends of TBI and SCI is already available. 19, 20 For example, plasma/serum glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) and ubiquitin C-terminal Hydrolase L1 (UCH-L1) increase immediately post-injury in response to astrocytic and neuronal cell injury/death and are cleared by the US Food and Drugs Administration to aid in the diagnosis of mild TBI and for determining need of a CT scan among adults. 21, 22 Additionally, plasma/serum neurofilament light chain (NfL) and total tau (t-tau) show promise as blood biomarkers of axonal injury. 23 However, these blood biomarkers are not ideal.

text.text: The most notable limitation is their inability to differentiate between common acute neurotrauma disorders such as TBI and SCI, as they are similarly elevated in both conditions. 24- 26 Moreover, plasma/serum GFAP, UCHL-1 and t-tau levels increase acutely, however contributions from systemic sources reduce confidence in diagnostic utility and specificity for central nervous system (CNS) disorders. 27, 28 Plasma NfL levels peak in the sub-acute period, limiting its use as an acute marker for rapid triage. 29 Additionally, the levels of these proteins are affected by co-morbid conditions and normal aging. [30] [31] [32] We recently described brain-derived tau (BD-tau), a novel blood-based biomarker that selectively recognizes tau protein isoforms released into blood circulation predominantly from the brain. 33, 34 This biomarker assay was designed to recognize the tau protein isoforms abundantly expressed in the adult human brain 34 while excluding the longer "big tau" isoforms predominantly produced outside of the brain, including peripheral nerves and neuronal components that project outside of the brain. [35] [36] [37] In fact, big tau makes up less than 1% of the total brain tau signal but accounts for the vast majority of non-CNS tau. 38 Additionally, big tau isoforms account for a larger proportion of the total amount of tau protein in the adult human spinal cord than the brain, providing a potential opportunity for differential diagnosis of disorders of the brain vs. spinal cord. 38 We hypothesized that baseline and longitudinal serum BD-tau levels will be distinctively sensitive to the diverging localization, clinical classification and outcome of acute TBI and SCI.

text.text: Here, we show that serum BD-tau concentrations accurately enable the differential diagnosis of TBI from SCI among patients admitted in a neuro-intensive care unit (ICU), with temporal dynamics over a six-day period robustly predictive of clinical severity and long-term functional outcomes specifically in TBI but not in SCI.
Importantly, serum BD-tau outperformed cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) BD-tau as well as serum NfL, GFAP and UCHL1 as a differential biomarker for acute neurotrauma.
Together, serum BD-tau uniquely captures biochemical signatures specific to CNS injury reflected in TBI but not in SCI.
Thus, serum BD-tau is a potential precision diagnostic tool to improve accessible neurotrauma care through accurate and rapid stratification of injury types.

This study included 364 total participants, with 342 neurotrauma patients admitted to the emergency department (ED) and/or intensive care unit (ICU) of the University of Pittsburgh Medical Center (UPMC) Trauma Center, Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, USA (n=285 TBI, n=57 SCI), and 22 healthy controls.

The TBI group included 12 mild, 6 moderate and 267 severe cases classified using the Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) criteria (mild: 13-15, moderate: 9-12, severe: 3-8), while the SCI group included 22 AISA-A, 7 AISA-B, 16 AISA-C and 4 AISA-D cases respectively based on the ASIA Impairment Scale (AIS) criteria, with AIS grade missing for 8 SCI cases (see Methods). 39, 40 The SCI subtypes C and D were grouped together for sample size purposes.

text.text: Serum BD-tau trajectories are associated with clinical outcomes after TBI Given the sustained elevation and heterogeneity of serum BD-tau trajectories among patients with TBI, longitudinal analyses showed distinct serum BD-tau trajectories by 3-month GOS outcome, with linear mixed-effects models identifying a significant outcome-by-time interaction for favorable versus unfavorable recovery (p = 0.022).

Patients with unfavorable outcomes generally exhibited higher serum BD-tau concentrations and slower declines over time, although individual timepoint comparisons were not significant after adjustment (Supplementary Table 4).

text.text: In this study, we have measured serum BD-tau by an immunoassay designed to selectively measure tau protein predominantly originating from the CNS in patients with acute neurotrauma.
This is the first reported investigation of BD-tau in SCI and the most comprehensive evaluation in TBI by injury severity, sample time-point and patient number, to date.
We have demonstrated that serum BD-tau can reliably differentiate the two common forms of neurotrauma diagnoses in the acute phase, with higher classification accuracy than CSF BD-tau.
Notably, serum BD-tau performed significantly superior to serum GFAP, UCH-L1and NfL, the most promising blood biomarkers for neurotrauma currently, in this context of use.
The superior performance of baseline serum BD-tau over GFAP, UCH-L1 and NfL in discriminating TBI from SCI is a novel finding.

CSF and blood levels of GFAP, UCH-L1, and NfL postinjury appear to capture shared pathophysiological and mechanistic processes between TBI and SCI. 13, [24] [25] [26] 42 GFAP and UCH-L1 are released into the bloodstream immediately following neurotrauma in response to astrocytic and neuronal damage.

text.text: For this reason, they have excellent utility for clinical diagnosis and predicting outcomes across TBI, SCI, and many other acute injury etiologies.

Furthermore, NfL, a marker of axonal injury, is released in the acute to sub-acute injury phase, reducing its utility in the immediate hours following TBI and SCI. 23, 43 The ubiquitousness of the temporal signatures of these proteins may limit their specificity for neurotrauma sub-types, and may explain why serum GFAP, NfL and UCHL-1 do not differentiate TBI from SCI as reliably.

text.text: The distinct serum BD-tau magnitude and temporal trajectory of TBI compared to SCI mirrors the diverging injury pathophysiology, including the mechanisms of injury, the tissue types affected, and thus the proteins released into the bloodstream.
Serum BD-tau more accurately discriminates between severe TBI and SCI compared to CSF BD-tau.

We hypothesize that this may be due to the release of this protein biomarker into systemic circulation following blood brain barrier damage after acute injury that circumvents ventricular drainage and proteins of CSF origin. 44 This is corroborated by the statistically significant correlation between serum and CSF BD-tau in TBI patients, which is consistent with previous reports of BD-tau correlations in paired serum and CSF in chronic neurodegeneration. 45, 46 These findings are similar to our previous results showing that plasma/serum GFAP is a better marker of microglia activation than CSF GFAP. 47 CSF tau appears relatively understudied, particularly in the severe TBI setting.

text.text: Altogether, BD-tau appears to reflect fundamental differences in injury biology and biomarker kinetics between TBI and SCI.
Measurements of serum BD-tau at 12-hour increments demonstrated differing temporal profiles between moderate/severe TBI (based on initial GCS score) and severe SCI patients.
Serum BD-tau levels decreased over time among the TBI patients with the rate of decline dependent on injury severity.
Moreover, no TBI group recovered to control levels within the six-day observation period, highlighting the high sensitivity of serum BD-tau to TBI even in less severe presentations.

Importantly, while baseline serum BD-tau levels were overlapping for moderate and severe TBI, the longitudinal profiling resolved that individuals with moderate TBI recorded faster serum BD-tau decreases at which point the levels remained high in the severe TBI cases.
This approach can be employed clinically to ascertain disease profiles and personalize treatment for TBI patients.

Conversely, and remarkably, serum BD-tau levels in SCI remained similar to baseline levels up to 144 hours post-injury and trajectories were similar across ASIA scores or injury location across the spine, indicating that this biomarker is indeed unchanged in SCI.
Serum BD-tau demonstrated distinct prognostic trajectories according to dichotomized longterm outcome classification, defined as unfavorable for GOS 1-3 and favorable for GOS 4-5.

While baseline serum BD-tau showed no differences in functional outcome, there was a significant difference in longitudinal trajectory up to 144 hours post-TBI when comparing patients with a favorable versus unfavorable outcome.

In a study of 1728 patients across 65 ICUs, fluid biomarker trajectories also had substantial discriminating power above clinical, physiological and imaging variables. 49 These results support clinical use of serial measurements of serum BD-tau to predict short-and long-term clinical outcomes among TBI patients.

text.text: Previous work has primarily focused on establishing prognostic and diagnostic utility of bloodbased biomarkers in TBI 50, 51 or SCI alone 52 .

text.text: By measuring and analyzing TBI and SCI concurrently, our results identify serum BD-tau as an accessible tool to support precision (differential) diagnosis of neurotrauma and to predict outcome among TBI patients.

The neurotrauma field aims to modernize characterization of acute TBI with the adaptation of the CBI-M framework. 53 In addition to the traditional application of clinical (C) and neuroimaging (I) classifications, the CBI-M approach aims to incorporate blood biomarkers (B) and external modifiers (M) to improve clinical management and treatment of TBI. 53 Our findings provide an opportunity to integrate BD-tau and other blood-based biomarkers into this multi-step workflow for acute neurotrauma care, in conjunction with standard clinical and imaging procedures.

text.text: For instance, following the generation and external validation of reference values, use of serum BD-tau could establish injury etiology, alongside established markers GFAP and UCH-L1.

Together, these findings advance biomarker efficacy in neurotrauma by directly focusing on the unmet clinical need for tools capable of differentially diagnosing these potential co-occurring injury types and improving outcomes following trauma.

This study has several strengths, including a pioneering direct evaluation of TBI and SCI patients in acute intensive care, the inclusion of a relatively large cohort, paired CSF and serum samples, cross-sectional and longitudinal assessments and comparison of serum BD-tau with hallmark blood-based biomarkers of neurotrauma.
A few limitations should be noted.

There are slight differences in the collection and processing of CSF and blood across the cohorts, primarily that CSF was collected via extra ventricular drain in TBI patients and from lumbar drain in SCI patients, in line with standard of care procedures. 54 While cell and protein count differ between ventricular and lumbar fluid 55 , tau levels appear to be comparable and highly correlated when directly compared. 56 Although this study represents the largest and most detailed evaluation of serum BD-tau in acute neurotrauma to date, larger studies are needed to increase statistical power for subgroup analyses and enhance generalizability of findings.

text.text: Future multicenter studies involving larger and more diverse populations, extended follow-up, and prospective validation will be required to establish the clinical utility of serum BD-tau.
In conclusion, serum BD-tau differentiating TBI from SCI is a novel finding and a significant step toward achieving precision diagnostics in acute neurotrauma patients.
Additionally, it can accelerate patient selection for therapeutic clinical trials and observational studies.
Finally, these findings demonstrate the potential of circulating biomarkers to improve precision diagnostics in acute neurotrauma care.

text.text: Patients were enrolled from 2012-2024 (n=285).
Subjects in the moderate TBI group, enrolled in the BTRC study, had an initial GCS score 9-10, but deteriorated to require intracranial monitoring (n=6).
Mild TBI cohort samples were obtained from patients admitted to the University of Pittsburgh Medical Center hospitals with reported trauma or brain injury.

Inclusion criteria include 1) Initial Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score of 13-15, (2) Age 18 or older, (3) The injury occurred less than 48 hours prior, (4) Loss of consciousness (LOC) and/or post-traumatic amnesia (PTA), (5) Reported mechanism of suspected TBI, and (6) Ability to obtain informed consent.

Exclusion criteria include: (1) Significant polytrauma that would interfere with follow-up and outcome assessment, (2) Pregnancy, (3) major debilitating baseline mental health disorders, pre-existing condition or neurological disease impairing baseline awareness, cognition that would interfere with follow-up and the validity of outcome assessment in the opinion of the principal investigator, (4) penetrating TBI, and (5) severe spinal cord injury.
Subjects were enrolled from 2018-2024 (n=12).
